excerpt: When you sign up for Google Voice, your organization gets a simple way to deploy and manage phone numbers at scale.
Users can link their number to any mobile or landline number and access Voice on their smartphones and computers.
Auto attendants—Design a menu system to direct callers to people or departments.
Desk phones—Set up desk phones for users to make and get Voice calls.
Track use and activity—Understand how your organization uses Voice.

If your organization has existing phone numbers with another service provider, you can port (or move) those numbers to Google Voice.
Landline or VoIP—Enter up to 1000 phone numbers (50 in Canada), separated by commas. For a number range, enter a starting and ending number separated by a hyphen.
In the Activation date field, click to open the calendar and choose when to activate the number.
If both domains are within the same Workspace account, you can unassign a number from a user in one domain and reassign it to a user in another domain
Multiple ports can be active at the same time. However, you cannot have more than one active simultaneous port from a single losing carrier account or BTN.
In other countries Google Voice provides a template to download for the customer to fill in with details matching the port order

You can set up ring groups to let people in your organization answer calls from the same Google Voice number.
Round robin—Rings each member in random order until someone answers.
Under Outbound callers, authorized users can place outbound calls using numbers assigned to the ring group.

A long-time user moved back to their regular cell number after development seemed dead for three years, with group MMS and picture message issues never fixed. They told friends to forget the GV number, and now only use it for sending test SMS from a computer.

A user who ported their mobile number to GV after moving to the UK says some SMS providers fail GV's 'is this a USA number' check. As a result it doesn't work with their US bank accounts, and they couldn't register for Lyft. They wish Google would charge a few bucks a month and staff it as a real product.
The user calls the old Google Voice app 'absolutely-awful' and says the Hangouts app taking over GV functionality was a lifeline.

The killer feature keeping this user on Google Voice is voicemail transcription emailed to their inbox. They set up their Verizon cell to use GV as voicemail even for direct calls. They still need the app to listen when transcription fails.
This user has been on Google Voice for about 7 years and never had issues. They felt the lack of updates was 'don't fix what isn't broken' and call transcribed voicemail a godsend.

This Fi user (with a number from Google Voice) says the phone sometimes doesn't ring before calls go to voicemail. No missed call shows; a voicemail just appears. There is no option to extend ringing time.
'One number for life' is undercut by needing to relinquish the GV number if you want to use Google Fi.
Because of Google's confusing moves, this user will always keep GV as a separate number. It's still very useful for texting and calling from any device or service.
The commenter's blunt verdict: 'Google voice for iOS is garbage.'
A Sprint user integrated their carrier number with Google Voice so all texts and calls sit in GV. They use the GV Chrome extension to reply to texts from their desktop.
The updated app has a cleaner interface and Spanish transcription is great. However, the update was underwhelming and slow to reach app stores.
A user who ported their number to Voice after leaving the US was frustrated by the lack of support. They tried Twilio with OpenVBX as an alternative, but that project seemed abandoned.
Commenters stress that Google can kill your phone number with no warning, no reason, and no recourse. They suggest users should at least get notice and time to port the number elsewhere.
A 10+ year user worries constantly about Google banning them or dropping the service. They want a paid alternative that works from the browser like Google Voice.
When this user first signed up, friends' test text messages never came through. They wrote GV off as unreliable and never used it.
Because free Google accounts can disappear without recourse, this user only gives their Google Voice number to likely spammers. They note a paid Workspace version of Voice exists.

One user warns against relying on Voice for anything critical. They say it shows the hallmarks of a destaffed project with no significant updates in years, and they only use it where they expect spam.

A ~15-year user runs Voice with a paid G Suite as their main inbound line for multiple numbers, MFA, and their professional number. They say it has been solid. They've found no alternative matching everything GV and its Android integration provide, but would be 'up a creek' if banned.

Several users say they ported their numbers away from Google Voice, after years of use, because they no longer trust Google's reliability or account bans. One suggests jmp.chat with an XMPP client as an alternative for calls and SMS.
A user who gives out their GV number as their main contact realized they have no backup of their Voice messages. They now plan regular backups.
